newsitem.title: USA: Ross to offer new U.S. ideas on Hebron.
newsitem.headline: Ross to offer new U.S. ideas on Hebron.

text.p: U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross will offer new American ideas aimed at pushing forward Israeli-Palestinian talks during a weekend trip to the region, the State Department said on Friday.

But spokesman Nicholas Burns said Ross's brief trip will aim mainly to revive the stalled talks on an Israeli troop withdrawal from the West Bank town of Hebron and was unlikely to produce an immediate agreement.

After more than 10 weeks of talks, the two sides remained deadlocked over security arrangements to protect some 400 Jews who live among 100,000 Arabs in Hebron, from which the Israelis were originally to have withdrawn last March.

Secretary of State Warren Christopher announced on Thursday that Ross, who was due to leave on Friday night for Israel, would be making the trip because of U.S. concerns over the "drift" in the Middle East peace process.

"Dennis is the primary intermediary between the two -- the Palestinians and the Israelis. He certainly has some ideas of his own -- American ideas that he will be offering on this trip," Burns told a news briefing.
Burns said Ross would spend only a few days in the region, returning to Washington next Tuesday.

"I think that perhaps the best we can hope for here is that he's able to convince (Palestinian) Chairman (Yasser) Arafat and (Israeli) Prime Minister (Benjamin) Netanyahu that they've got to re-engage seriously on Hebron."
"It may take some more time, however, for any final agreement to be reached," he said.
Despite reports quoting U.S. ambassador to Israel Martin Indyk as saying a Hebron deal was essentially complete, Burns said he thought there were still "a few remaining issues."
Burns said Ross would meet only Israelis and Palestinians and would not visit Syria or Jordan.

The U.S. spokesman also denied that a statement by Christopher on Thursday that the Palestinians should respond to Israeli offers on Hebron did not mean Washington was softening its criticism of Jewish settlements in the West Bank.
President Bill Clinton said on Monday the settlements, which Netanyahu's government is expanding, were "absolutely" an obstacle to peace.
